title: The consonants
hook: a tissue held to a kid's lips jumps when she says dhamma right
tomorrow: namo tassa: homage to him. so why not just say his name?

segments.voice: Yesterday, the vowels: short stays short, long gets its time. Open vowels. And a question was left hanging: why does dhamma carry an h you can barely hear?

Sunday morning, a temple hall, a row of kids cross-legged on the carpet. The teacher holds a tissue an inch from one girl's lips. Say dhamma. Damma, she says. The tissue hangs still. Again, says the teacher, with the breath. Dhamma. This time the tissue jumps, the whole row laughs, and the girl grins like she just won something. That jump is the answer to yesterday's question. The h in dhamma isn't a letter you hear by itself. It's breath, and you can feel it.
screen: `A TISSUE AT HER LIPS.` → `DAMMA: NOTHING MOVES.` → `DHAMMA: IT JUMPS.`

segments.voice: Pali writes breath into the spelling. Many of its consonants come in pairs: a plain sound, and the same sound with a puff of air. k and kh. g and gh. t and th. d and dh. p and ph. b and bh. The h never stands alone; it rides on the letter before it. Two surprises hide there. Pali th is never the th of think: it's a t with breath behind it. And ph is never the f of phone: it's a p with a puff. Now say Buddha. On the page there's a d, then a dh. The first one holds; the second lets the breath go. The same breath opens dhamma, and bhagavato, the word that follows namo tassa in the homage. Then there's a second family: sounds made with the tip of the tongue curled back toward the roof of the mouth. In roman letters they wear a small dot underneath. Tipitaka, the three baskets of the canon, has both kinds of t in one word: the first with the tongue at the teeth, the second curled back. English leaves breath and tongue to chance. Pali spells them out, so a chanter reading the page knows where the breath goes. A breath in the word, written down so it isn't lost.
screen: `PLAIN AND BREATHY: D AND DH.` · `TH IS NOT THINK. PH IS NOT PHONE.` · `BUDDHA: HOLD, THEN BREATHE.` · `A DOT BENEATH: THE TONGUE CURLS BACK.` · then, large: `A BREATH IN THE WORD.`

segments.voice: Hold your palm an inch from your lips. Say damma, plain, and then dhamma, with the breath, and feel the small puff land on your hand. Go back and forth slowly a few times, then let the hand rest in your lap and sit with the breath that was in the word all along.
The consonants. Plain ones and breathy ones, like d and dh, and the tongue-curled ones that carry a dot beneath. Word three of a little Pali.
The line for today: a breath in the word, the h you feel more than hear. Day three of the block, done.

howItsDone: Pali chanting books in roman letters write the breathy consonants with an h and mark the tongue-curled ones with a dot beneath; new chanters learn them by ear, chanting along with monks and longtime lay chanters.

pairs: a d with a puff of breath
a t with breath, never the th of think
a p with a puff, never an f

myth: the h in dhamma is silent
it's a puff of breath riding on the d; hold your palm up and you can feel it.
Pali ph sounds like the f in phone
it's a p with a puff of air after it, never an f.
a dot under t, d or n marks a tongue-curled sound
in roman letters, the dot beneath means the tip of the tongue curls back toward the roof of the mouth.

fork.setup: you're lettering a chant poster and the h's are crowding your design: dhamma, Buddha, bhagavato. what do you cut?
options: nothing: each h tells the chanter where a breath goes.
the h's: they're silent, so the chant sounds the same.
every other h: chanters will pick up the pattern.
fork.reveal: the h isn't decoration. dh, bh and the rest are breathy sounds, and the spelling is how a chanter reading the page knows to breathe them.

original.note: dhamma in Devanagari letters: ध is the breathy dh, written as one letter, not d plus h.

trapdoor: what you thought: the h in dhamma and Buddha is a silent leftover.
what it means: Pali writes breath into the word: kh, gh, th, dh, ph and bh are each one sound with a puff.
what a scholar hears: in Indian scripts each breathy consonant is a single letter of its own; roman spelling borrows an h to show the breath.
guess: the plain, breathy and curled sounds of Pali
the silent letters chanters skip to keep pace
the hard sounds only monks learn to say aloud

chat.says: lettered DAMMA across the big poster. a kid at class said it's missing something. is it?
options: Yes, the h. In dhamma it's a puff of breath on the d, so the poster needs it.
No. The h is silent in Pali, so leaving it off the poster changes nothing.
Kind of. The h just means say it louder, so it's fine either way.
chat.meaning: Pali writes breath into the spelling: dh is a d with a puff of air. The h tells a chanter where the breath goes.

dhamma.meaning: the Buddha's teaching; its dh is a d with breath

Buddha.meaning: the awakened one; spelled with a d, then a breathy dh

bhagavato.meaning: to the Blessed One: the word after namo tassa

Tipitaka.meaning: the three baskets: the Pali canon

notes: The hook's tissue scene is an illustration, not a reported custom; the tissue (or palm) test is a common way to feel aspiration. Confirm it reads as a plain classroom scene.

Outline hook says the tongue-curled and breathy sounds are 'heard in dhamma and Buddha'; in fact both words carry the dental aspirate dh (breathy), not a retroflex. The script uses dhamma and Buddha for the breath and Tipitaka (ti- dental t, -ṭaka retroflex ṭ) for the curled sound. Keeper: confirm the Tipitaka example and spelling.
'Pali th is never the th of think; ph is never the f of phone': standard pronunciation guidance in Pali grammars; paraphrased. Confirm.
'Many of its consonants come in pairs' refers to the five plain/aspirated pairs per stop row; stated loosely on purpose. Buddha written d + dh (buddha) per standard spelling.
Original: ध as a single Devanagari letter for dh; confirm.
